title: Building AI Agents for Coding
description: Go beyond chat and learn to build practical AI agents that can execute multi-step coding tasks with tools and memory.

data.text: What Does Building an AI Agent Mean?

Building an AI coding agent does not necessarily mean writing code from scratch. It means configuring or programming an existing agent framework to perform coding tasks autonomously. This includes giving the agent tools (file operations, shell commands, API calls), setting up memory so it can track progress, and defining guardrails to keep it on track.

data.title: Every practical coding agent has these components:
items: LLM — the reasoning engine that plans and makes decisions
Tools — file read/write/edit, shell commands, API calls, search
Memory — short-term (conversation history) and long-term (project context)
Guardrails — rules that prevent destructive actions
Loop — the Plan-Execute-Verify cycle that drives the agent

data.text: The tools an agent can use define what it can accomplish. For coding agents, the essential tools are: read file, write file, edit file, run shell command, run tests, and search codebase. More advanced tools include API calls, database queries, and deployment commands. Each tool needs a clear description of what it does and what parameters it accepts.

data.title: Tool descriptions matter
data.text: The LLM decides which tool to use based on the description you provide. A vague description like 'run a command' will result in unpredictable behavior. A precise description like 'Run a shell command in the project root and return the first 50 lines of output. Use for running tests, linters, or build commands.' produces much more reliable tool selection.

Coding agents need two types of memory. Short-term memory is the conversation history — what the agent has done in the current session. Long-term memory is the project context — the agent's knowledge of the codebase structure, coding conventions, and architecture decisions. Without long-term memory, the agent treats every session as a fresh start and repeatedly makes the same mistakes.

Guardrails are rules that prevent the agent from taking destructive actions. For coding agents, common guardrails include: do not delete files without explicit confirmation, do not run commands that modify the system outside the project directory, do not access environment variables with secrets, and always ask before force-pushing. Guardrails are especially important when using autonomous agents that can run without human oversight.

data.title: Frameworks and tools for building coding agents:
items: LangChain / LangGraph — Python/TypeScript framework for building LLM applications with tools and memory
OpenAI Assistants API — GPT-4 with built-in code interpretation and file search
Anthropic Tool Use — Claude with structured tool definitions
AutoGPT / BabyAGI — autonomous agent frameworks (experimental for coding)
Cursor Composer / GitHub Copilot Workspace — pre-built coding agents for IDE use

data.title: Minimal agent for coding tasks:
items: Define the goal: 'Write unit tests for the UserService module'
List the tools: read_file, write_file, run_command (for pytest)
Set up the LLM with a system prompt that describes the tools
Initialize short-term memory with the project structure
Run the loop: plan which files to test, read them, generate tests, run them, fix failures

data.text: Measure agent performance by tracking: task completion rate (does it finish what it starts?), steps to completion (how many iterations to succeed?), and human interventions (how often do you need to step in?). A good agent for coding should complete simple tasks without intervention and ask for help on complex tasks rather than failing silently.

data.title: Example agent prompt configuration
data.content:
System prompt:
"You are a coding agent specialized in Python testing. You have access to read_file, write_file, and run_command tools. Always run the test suite after writing tests and fix any failures. If a test fails, read the error, identify the issue, and fix the test or the implementation. Do not modify files outside the tests/ directory without explicit approval."

Goal: "Write comprehensive pytest tests for the UserService class in src/services/user_service.py"
data.code:
System prompt:
"You are a coding agent specialized in Python testing. You have access to `read_file`, `write_file`, and `run_command` tools. Always run the test suite after writing tests and fix any failures. If a test fails, read the error, identify the issue, and fix the test or the implementation. Do not modify files outside the `tests/` directory without explicit approval."

Goal: "Write comprehensive pytest tests for the `UserService` class in `src/services/user_service.py`"

data.title: Start with constrained tasks
data.text: Do not give an agent a broad, open-ended goal like 'improve the codebase.' Start with narrow, well-defined tasks: 'Write tests for the UserService class' or 'Refactor the dataProcessor function.' Constrained tasks let you evaluate the agent's capabilities and build trust before giving it larger responsibilities.

data.title: Building AI agents for coding
points: Agents need LLM, tools, memory, guardrails, and a loop
Tool descriptions must be precise for reliable behavior
Memory prevents the agent from repeating mistakes
